questions.question: What are the core Redis data structures and when would you use each one in a Java application?
questions.title: Redis Data Structures: String, Hash, List, Set, ZSet, and Stream
questions.direct_answer: Redis offers six primary data structures — String, Hash, List, Set, Sorted Set (ZSet), and Stream — each optimized for specific access patterns. Strings handle simple key-value caching and counters, Hashes model objects efficiently, Lists support queues and stacks, Sets enforce uniqueness, Sorted Sets power leaderboards and range queries, and Streams handle event sourcing. Choosing the right structure directly impacts memory usage and query performance.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate understands Redis beyond simple string caching and can map data structures to real use cases.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Candidates often default to using String for everything, missing memory savings and richer operations available from Hashes or Sets.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention time complexity for each structure's core operations and give a concrete Java/Spring example for at least two structures.

sections.title: How it works under the hood
sections.content:
Redis is fundamentally different from a plain key-value store because its value side supports rich data structures, each backed by purpose-built algorithms. Strings use simple dynamic strings (SDS) internally and support atomic increment, bit operations, and binary payloads up to 512 MB, making them the default for session tokens, counters, and serialized object caches. Hashes store field-value maps and use a compact listpack encoding when the field count stays below `hash-max-listpack-entries` (default 128), which saves roughly 10× memory compared to individual String keys per field — a detail that matters at scale when you model millions of user profiles.

Lists are doubly-linked under the hood (quicklist of listpacks since Redis 7), giving O(1) push/pop at both ends while keeping small lists memory-efficient. This makes them natural candidates for notification feeds, recent-activity timelines, and simple work queues paired with `BRPOP` for blocking consumers. Sets use a hash table internally (or intset for small integer-only sets) and shine when you need uniqueness guarantees — tracking online users, computing mutual friends via `SINTER`, or tagging systems where tag membership must be deduplicated.

Sorted Sets combine a skip list with a hash table, yielding O(log N) insertion and O(log N + M) range queries. The dual index lets you look up a member's score in O(1) via the hash table while the skip list maintains order — this is why leaderboard rank lookups and score updates are both fast even with millions of members. Streams, added in Redis 5, model an append-only log with consumer group semantics inspired by Kafka: `XREADGROUP` delivers entries to consumers, `XACK` acknowledges processing, and the stream can be trimmed with `MAXLEN` or `MINID`. Choosing the right structure is the single most impactful design decision when integrating Redis, because it determines memory footprint, command complexity, and whether your access pattern can be served in a single round-trip or requires multiple commands.

sections.content:
- **String with `INCR` for atomic counters** — `INCR` is atomic even under thousands of concurrent clients; the foundation for rate limiters, hit counters, and distributed sequence generators
- **Hash for object field access without full deserialization** — `HGET user:123 email` retrieves one field; more efficient than deserializing a JSON blob when only one attribute is needed
- **List with `BRPOP` as a simple job queue** — blocking pop waits for an item; producers `LPUSH`, consumers `BRPOP`; use Redis Streams when you need consumer groups and acknowledgment
- **Sorted Set for ranked data** — `ZADD` with a score; `ZREVRANGE` returns members in descending score order; natural for leaderboards, priority queues, and expiring entries via timestamp score
- **Stream for durable event logs with consumer groups** — each consumer group maintains its own read position; unacknowledged messages can be reclaimed; fills the gap between List queues and Kafka

sections.title: How to explain this in an interview
sections.content:
Redis provides six core data structures, and choosing the right one for a given problem is what separates effective Redis usage from treating it as a simple key-value store.

**String — the universal type**
- String is the most basic type — it holds text, numbers, or binary data up to 512MB; `SET key value EX 3600` stores a value with a 1-hour TTL in one command
- `INCR` and `INCRBY` on string values are atomic — which means a rate limiter or counter can be safely incremented from thousands of concurrent clients without a race condition

**Hash — for objects with multiple fields**
- A Redis Hash maps field names to values within one key — `HSET user:123 name "Alice" email "alice@example.com"` stores multiple attributes under one key, allowing `HGET user:123 name` to retrieve individual fields without deserializing the whole object
- More memory-efficient than storing a serialized JSON string when you need to update individual fields frequently

**List — for queues and feeds**
- List maintains insertion order; `LPUSH` and `RPUSH` add to left or right; `BRPOP` blocks until an item is available — which makes it a natural message queue pattern for background job dispatch

**Set and Sorted Set (ZSet)**
- Set holds unique members and supports set operations — `SADD`, `SUNION`, `SINTER`, `SDIFF` — useful for tags, friend lists, or deduplication
- Sorted Set (ZSet) associates each member with a score and keeps members ordered by score — which means `ZADD leaderboard 4500 "alice"` then `ZREVRANGE leaderboard 0 9` returns the top 10 in one command; the natural structure for real-time rankings and scheduled tasks by timestamp

**Stream — for event logs**
- Stream provides a persistent, ordered log of entries with consumer group semantics — similar to a lightweight Kafka topic, useful for event sourcing, activity feeds, and reliable message delivery with acknowledgment

questions.question: How do you implement caching in Spring Boot using the @Cacheable and @CacheEvict annotations with Redis?
questions.title: Spring Cache Abstraction with Redis (@Cacheable, @CacheEvict)
questions.direct_answer: Spring's cache abstraction lets you declaratively add Redis caching to any Spring bean method using @Cacheable to cache results, @CachePut to update the cache, and @CacheEvict to invalidate entries — all without mixing caching logic into business code. You configure a RedisCacheManager bean to connect Spring's abstraction to Redis, set TTLs per cache, and choose a serializer. The result is clean service code where caching is a cross-cutting concern managed by AOP proxies.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical knowledge of wiring Spring caching to Redis, including configuration, key generation, and cache eviction strategies.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Forgetting to add @EnableCaching on the configuration class, or not configuring a custom KeyGenerator, leading to key collisions between methods.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the proxy-based limitation (self-invocation doesn't hit the cache), custom key expressions with SpEL, and how to configure per-cache TTLs.

sections.title: How it works under the hood
sections.content:
Spring's cache abstraction decouples caching logic from business code using an AOP proxy model. When the application context starts, Spring scans for `@Cacheable`, `@CachePut`, and `@CacheEvict` annotations and wraps the annotated beans in a proxy. On every call to a `@Cacheable` method, the proxy intercepts the invocation, computes the cache key from the method arguments (using SpEL if specified), and checks the configured `CacheManager`. If the key exists, the cached value is returned without invoking the target method. On a miss, the method executes, and the return value is stored in the cache for future calls.

The `RedisCacheManager` bridges Spring's abstraction to Redis. Under the hood it uses `RedisTemplate` to serialize keys and values, store them as Redis Strings with an optional TTL, and prefix every key with the cache name to avoid collisions across different `@Cacheable` targets. Configuring per-cache TTLs is critical in production: a user-profile cache might tolerate 30 minutes of staleness, while a pricing cache might need a 60-second TTL to stay fresh during promotions.

The most common pitfall is the proxy-based self-invocation trap. Because Spring intercepts calls at the proxy boundary, a method calling another `@Cacheable` method on `this` bypasses the cache entirely — the call never passes through the proxy. The fix is to inject a self-reference or extract the cached method into a separate bean. Another subtlety is key collisions: if two different methods share the same cache name and happen to receive identical arguments, their entries collide. Using explicit `key` expressions with `#root.methodName` or a custom `KeyGenerator` prevents this. Finally, `@Cacheable(sync = true)` tells Spring to synchronize cache population for a given key, which mitigates cache stampedes when a hot key expires under high concurrency.

sections.title: Step 1 — Add Dependencies
sections.content:
Add the Redis starter and Spring cache dependencies to your build file:

```xml
<!-- pom.xml -->
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-data-redis</artifactId>
</dependency>
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-cache</artifactId>
</dependency>
```

```yaml
# application.yml — Redis connection
spring:
  data:
    redis:
      host: localhost
      port: 6379
      password: ${REDIS_PASSWORD:}
      lettuce:
        pool:
          max-active: 16
          max-idle: 8
```

Spring Boot auto-configures a `LettuceConnectionFactory` from these properties. The Lettuce client is non-blocking and thread-safe, so a single connection factory serves the entire application.

Key Points
sections.content:
- **`@Cacheable` skips method execution on cache hit** — first call executes and caches; subsequent calls return cached value; method body is never reached again until the cache expires or is evicted
- **`@CacheEvict` after writes prevents stale reads** — annotate the update and delete methods with eviction; without eviction, the cache returns the old value until the TTL expires
- **`@CachePut` keeps cache warm on writes** — always executes the method and updates the cache; combine with `@CacheEvict` or use instead of it when you want the updated value immediately cached
- **Always configure TTL on caches** — without TTL, Redis entries persist until evicted; a service restart or deployment doesn't clear them; stale data can survive arbitrarily long
- **Cache key collisions cause silent bugs** — if two methods share the same cache name and key expression, one method's cached value is returned for the other; use distinct cache names or key expressions per method

sections.title: How to explain this in an interview
sections.content:
Spring's cache abstraction lets you add Redis caching to any Spring bean method with three annotations — `@Cacheable`, `@CachePut`, and `@CacheEvict` — without coupling the business logic to the caching implementation.

**`@Cacheable` — cache on first call**
- Place `@Cacheable(value = "products", key = "#id")` on a method — on the first call, the method executes and the return value is stored in Redis under the key `products::id`; subsequent calls with the same argument return the cached value without executing the method
- The cache key defaults to the method parameters; use SpEL expressions to compose custom keys: `key = "#user.id + ':' + #status"`

**`@CacheEvict` — invalidate on mutation**
- Place `@CacheEvict(value = "products", key = "#id")` on a service method that updates or deletes a product — when that method executes, Spring removes the corresponding Redis key so the next read fetches fresh data
- `allEntries = true` evicts every key in the named cache — useful after a bulk import that invalidates everything

**`@CachePut` — update the cache on write**
- `@CachePut` always executes the method AND updates the cache — unlike `@Cacheable` which skips the method on a hit; use it on create or update methods to keep the cache warm

**Configuration in Spring Boot**
- Add `spring-boot-starter-data-redis` and configure `spring.redis.host`; add `@EnableCaching` to the application; Spring Boot auto-configures a `RedisCacheManager` using Jackson for serialization
- Configure TTL per cache: `RedisCacheConfiguration.defaultCacheConfig().entryTtl(Duration.ofMinutes(10))` — without TTL, cached values live until evicted, which can cause stale data to persist indefinitely

questions.question: What are the differences between cache-aside, write-through, and write-behind caching strategies?
questions.title: Cache-Aside vs Write-Through vs Write-Behind Caching Strategies
questions.direct_answer: Cache-aside (lazy loading) puts cache management in application code: read from cache, fall back to DB on miss, then populate the cache. Write-through keeps cache and DB always in sync by writing to both on every update, at the cost of write latency. Write-behind (write-back) writes to the cache immediately and asynchronously flushes to the DB, boosting write throughput but risking data loss on crash. The right choice depends on your read/write ratio and tolerance for stale data or data loss.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of caching patterns beyond simple 'cache the result', including trade-offs between consistency, latency, and durability.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing write-through with write-behind, or not considering what happens on a cache miss in each strategy.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention read-through as a variant of cache-aside where the cache itself handles DB reads, and discuss which strategies pair well with Redis vs Memcached.

sections.title: Read-through, refresh-ahead, and operational nuance
sections.content:
Read-through caching moves miss handling into the cache layer: the store calls the database loader itself, which simplifies application code compared to classic cache-aside but couples you to a cache implementation that understands your entity loader. Refresh-ahead proactively reloads keys before they expire when access predictions show they will be hot again—useful for catalog edges that spike predictably, but it can over-fetch if predictions are wrong.

When you evaluate strategies for a Spring Boot service, quantify **read:write ratio**, **staleness budget**, and **durability**. Cache-aside keeps the database authoritative and is forgiving when Redis disappears—you simply pay more database load until the cache refills. Write-through shines when product owners insist the cache never serves a version older than the primary row, such as pricing during a promotion, at the cost of synchronously touching two systems on every mutation. Write-back is rarely the default: reserve it for extremely write-heavy, loss-tolerant workloads where asynchronous writers and replay queues are already part of your reliability story.

Finally, operational concerns overlap all patterns: observability on hit ratio, tracing cache misses to downstream latency, and drills for "Redis down" should appear in the same answer as the strategy names—interviewers want proof you shipped this, not just memorized definitions. Understanding these patterns in the context of Spring Boot specifically helps frame the interview answer. With `@Cacheable`, Spring implements cache-aside transparently via AOP.

sections.title: Strategy Comparison
sections.content:
| Aspect | Cache-Aside (Lazy) | Write-Through | Write-Behind (Write-Back) |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Read path** | Check cache → miss → query DB → populate cache | Check cache → always hit (cache is pre-populated) | Check cache → always hit (cache is pre-populated) |
| **Write path** | Write DB → evict/update cache | Write cache + DB synchronously | Write cache → async flush to DB |
| **Consistency** | Eventual (stale until TTL or eviction) | Strong (cache always matches DB) | Eventual (async lag) |
| **Write latency** | DB latency only (cache update is fire-and-forget) | DB + cache latency (both synchronous) | Cache latency only (DB write deferred) |
| **Data loss risk** | None (DB is authoritative) | None (DB always written) | **Yes** — crash before flush loses buffered writes |
| **Memory efficiency** | High (only hot data cached) | Low (all written data cached, even if never read) | Low (all written data cached) |
| **Complexity** | Simple (app controls everything) | Medium (cache must front every write) | High (needs async queue, retry, ordering) |
| **Best for** | Read-heavy, tolerance for brief staleness | Read-heavy, zero-staleness requirement | Write-heavy, loss-tolerant (leaderboards, analytics) |
| **Spring support** | `@Cacheable` + `@CacheEvict` | `@CachePut` on every mutation | Custom `RedisTemplate` + async processor |

sections.title: Cache-Aside Pattern in Java
Key Points
sections.content:
- **Cache-aside is the safest default** — cache holds only requested data; simple miss/fill logic; risk is cache stampede on simultaneous cold misses; mitigate with probabilistic early expiry or a distributed lock on fill
- **Write-through eliminates stale reads at the cost of write speed** — cache always reflects the latest write; every write takes two round trips (cache + database); wasted cache space for data never read
- **Write-behind risks data loss** — database writes are async; a Redis failure between write and async flush loses the update permanently; appropriate only when some loss is acceptable (counters, metrics)
- **TTL is required in all strategies** — without TTL, cache-aside entries are never evicted when the database changes without a corresponding cache write; always set a reasonable expiry
- **Mixing strategies introduces inconsistency** — if some write paths evict and others don't, or some reads use cache while others bypass it, the cache reflects a partial view; enforce the strategy consistently across all paths to the same data

sections.title: How to explain this in an interview
sections.content:
Cache strategies differ in who fills the cache and when — and choosing the wrong strategy leads to either stale data (write-behind) or cache misses at the worst time (cache-aside on cold start).

**Cache-aside (lazy loading) — the most common**
- The application checks the cache first; on a miss, it queries the database, stores the result in the cache, and returns it — which means the cache only holds data that's been requested, so cold start doesn't pre-populate anything
- This is the right default for most read-heavy workloads: simple to implement, no wasted cache space on data that's never read
- The risk is cache stampede on cold start or after expiry: many concurrent requests all miss simultaneously, all hit the database, and all try to write the same key — handled with probabilistic early expiry or a mutex

**Write-through — always update cache on write**
- The application writes to the cache and the database together — which means the cache is always warm and reads are always fast, but writes are slower (two writes instead of one) and cache entries exist even for data that's never read
- Best when you can't afford a cache miss for any user — payment processing, real-time inventory, user session data

**Write-behind (write-back) — write to cache first, database later**
- Writes go to the cache immediately and the database asynchronously in the background — which means writes are extremely fast but the database may be temporarily behind, and a Redis crash before the async flush loses those writes
- Only appropriate for high-throughput write scenarios where some data loss is acceptable: analytics counters, activity feeds, approximate metrics

**Read-through — the cache fetches from the database itself**
- The application always reads from the cache; on a miss, the cache automatically queries the database and populates itself — the application code doesn't handle misses explicitly; used in Redis caching middleware like AWS ElastiCache with DAX

questions.question: When would you choose Redis over Memcached, and what are the key differences?
questions.title: Redis vs Memcached: Choosing the Right Cache
questions.direct_answer: Redis is a feature-rich in-memory data store supporting multiple data structures, persistence, pub/sub, Lua scripting, and clustering, while Memcached is a simpler, multi-threaded key-value cache focused purely on raw throughput. Choose Memcached when you need the absolute fastest simple string caching with multiple CPU cores; choose Redis when you need persistence, richer data structures, atomic operations, or Spring Boot's first-class integration via spring-data-redis.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate can articulate concrete technical differences rather than just saying 'Redis has more features'.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Saying Memcached is 'worse' without acknowledging its genuine advantages in raw multi-threaded throughput for simple use cases.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that Redis is single-threaded for command processing (but uses I/O threads in Redis 6+), and that Memcached's multi-threaded model can outperform Redis for pure string GET/SET at very high concurrency.

sections.title: Operational comparison beyond the feature matrix
sections.content:
In production the decision is rarely a micro-benchmark of raw `GET` throughput alone. Memcached shines when teams operate a fleet of stateless app servers that only need a shared byte bucket for HTML fragments or precomputed JSON blobs, and when horizontal scale of the cache tier itself is solved purely by adding more independent nodes with consistent hashing in the client.

Redis adds operational surface—replication lag monitoring, AOF rewrite spikes, cluster resharding—but pays back with primitives that remove entire categories of infrastructure. A single Redis can be the coordination point for rate limits, feature flags, leaderboards, and session storage, which lowers the number of systems on call engineers must reason about during incidents.

For Java services specifically, serialization format and connection pooling dominate tail latency more often than the cache engine choice. A Memcached client that serializes with verbose JSON may lose its throughput advantage over Lettuce talking Redis with compact binary protocols. Mention **SLA on data loss** explicitly: Memcached drops everything on restart unless you rebuild from elsewhere; Redis persistence gives you a warm-ish restart path when configured responsibly.

When Memcached still wins, say so clearly: extremely parallel simple workloads where Redis command serialization would bottleneck, or organizations that already standardized Memcached SRE playbooks. Showing both sides reads as senior judgment rather than framework cheerleading.

sections.content:
Memcached and Redis both cache data in memory, and for the specific use case of caching serialized objects with a TTL, either works. The differences become significant when you need anything beyond that.

**Memcached — built for maximum throughput on one job**
- Memcached was designed from the ground up to be the fastest distributed cache for string key-value pairs — it's multi-threaded, highly optimized for that single use case, and nothing else
- It supports only String values; no data structure operations; no persistence; no pub/sub; no scripting; no replication; no atomic operations beyond `INCR`/`DECR`

**Redis — a data structure server**
- Redis is not just a cache — it's a data structure server that supports Strings, Hashes, Lists, Sets, Sorted Sets, and Streams, each with purpose-built atomic operations
- Redis is single-threaded for command execution (multi-threaded for I/O in Redis 6+), which means command ordering is deterministic — `INCR` on a counter is always atomic, making it safe for rate limiting and distributed counters
- Redis supports persistence (RDB snapshots, AOF log), replication, Cluster mode for horizontal scaling, and pub/sub — making it a complete data platform, not just a cache

**Why Redis won**
- Redis's richer feature set covers caching, session storage, rate limiting, pub/sub, queues, and leaderboards in one tool — teams avoid running both Redis and a message broker for simple queue needs
- The throughput difference between Redis and Memcached is negligible for most web applications; the operational simplicity of one tool for many purposes has made Redis the default choice

questions.question: How do you implement distributed locking in Java using Redisson, and what pitfalls should you avoid?
questions.title: Distributed Locking with Redisson in Spring Boot
questions.direct_answer: Redisson provides a RLock implementation that uses the Redlock algorithm to acquire a distributed lock across Redis nodes, ensuring mutual exclusion across JVM instances. You call lock.tryLock() with a wait time and lease time, execute your critical section, and release in a finally block. Key pitfalls include not releasing the lock in a finally block, setting lease times too short relative to the critical section duration, and using a single Redis node instead of RedLock's majority-quorum approach for strong guarantees.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical experience with distributed coordination problems and the specific challenges of lock expiry, clock skew, and crash scenarios.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using SETNX directly without an expiry, which can leave orphaned locks if the process crashes, permanently blocking other nodes.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Discuss the Martin Kleppmann vs Salvatore Sanfilippo debate about Redlock's safety guarantees and mention fencing tokens as a complement to Redlock.

sections.title: How it works under the hood
sections.content:
Distributed locking solves a coordination problem that arises whenever multiple JVM instances need mutual exclusion over a shared resource — for example, ensuring that only one instance processes a payment, sends a notification, or runs a scheduled batch at any given time. Redis is a natural fit because its single-threaded command execution makes `SET key value NX PX ttl` inherently atomic: the key is set only if it does not already exist, and the TTL ensures automatic cleanup if the holder crashes.

Redisson's `RLock` builds on this primitive with several production-grade features. The watchdog mechanism is the most important: when you call `lock()` without a lease time, Redisson spawns a background Netty timer that renews the lock's TTL every `lockWatchdogTimeout / 3` milliseconds (default ~10 seconds) as long as the owning thread is alive. This prevents the lock from expiring while the critical section is still executing due to GC pauses, network delays, or slow I/O. If the JVM crashes, the watchdog dies with it and the lock TTL expires naturally, avoiding orphaned locks.

The Redlock algorithm, proposed by Redis's author, extends single-node locking to N independent Redis instances. The client attempts to acquire the lock on each instance within a bounded time window and considers the lock acquired only if a majority (N/2 + 1) succeed. This tolerates the failure of any minority of nodes. However, Martin Kleppmann's analysis showed that Redlock's safety relies on bounded clock drift and process pauses — assumptions that real systems can violate. For truly critical paths (financial transfers, inventory decrements), the industry consensus is to complement the lock with a fencing token: a monotonically increasing counter attached to the lock that downstream systems check before accepting writes, so a delayed holder that lost the lock cannot perform a stale write.

sections.title: Step 1 — Add Redisson Dependency
sections.content:
Add Redisson to your Maven or Gradle build:

```xml
<!-- pom.xml -->
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.redisson</groupId>
    <artifactId>redisson-spring-boot-starter</artifactId>
    <version>3.27.0</version>
</dependency>
```

Redisson bundles its own Redis client (based on Netty) and provides distributed implementations of `java.util.concurrent` structures — `Lock`, `Semaphore`, `CountDownLatch`, `ReadWriteLock`, and more. The starter auto-configures a `RedissonClient` bean from `application.yml`.

Key Points
sections.content:
- **`SET key NX EX` is fragile on failover** — if the Redis primary fails after setting the key before replication, the new primary has no record of the lock; Redlock on N independent instances prevents this
- **Redlock requires majority quorum** — acquire on at least N/2 + 1 of N independent Redis nodes; a single node failure doesn't break the lock because the majority still holds it
- **Redisson watchdog renews the TTL automatically** — the watchdog thread extends the lease every 10s while the holder is alive; stops renewing on process death so the lock expires naturally without a crashed holder blocking forever
- **Always set a lease time** — a lock with no TTL causes permanent blocking if the holder crashes; set lease time longer than the longest expected critical section plus safety margin
- **Prefer database optimistic locking for most cases** — `@Version` in JPA with `OptimisticLockException` retry is simpler and avoids Redis dependency for mutual exclusion on database records

sections.title: How to explain this in an interview
sections.content:
Distributed locking with Redis is a common interview topic because it looks simple but has real failure modes. The naive implementation — `SET key NX EX 30` — works in single-node Redis but not across a cluster under failure scenarios.

**Why the naive `SETNX` approach is fragile**
- `SET key NX EX 30` creates a key only if it doesn't exist, with a 30-second TTL — which means the first caller acquires the lock and others fail fast; this works on a single Redis instance
- The problem: if the Redis primary fails after the key is set but before the replica replicates it, a new primary is elected without the lock key, and a second caller acquires the lock — two holders of the "exclusive" lock simultaneously

**Redlock — the multi-node algorithm**
- Redlock acquires the lock on N independent Redis instances (not a cluster) — for a lock to be held, it must be acquired on a majority (N/2 + 1) of instances; a single instance failure doesn't break the lock because the majority still holds it
- Redisson implements Redlock in Java with `RLock` — `lock.tryLock(waitTime, leaseTime, TimeUnit.SECONDS)` handles the multi-instance coordination automatically

**Lease time and watchdog**
- Every distributed lock needs a TTL to prevent a crashed holder from holding the lock forever — Redisson's `RLock` defaults to a 30-second lease and a watchdog thread that renews the TTL every 10 seconds while the holder is alive
- The watchdog stops renewing if the application process dies — which means the lock eventually expires naturally, and other holders can acquire it

**When distributed locking is overkill**
- For most application-level mutual exclusion, optimistic locking with a database version column is simpler and doesn't require Redis — use `@Version` in JPA; a conflicting update throws `OptimisticLockException` and the caller retries

questions.question: What is the difference between RDB and AOF persistence in Redis, and how do you choose between them?
questions.title: Redis Persistence: RDB vs AOF
questions.direct_answer: RDB (Redis Database) takes point-in-time snapshots of the dataset at configurable intervals, producing compact binary files ideal for backups and fast restarts. AOF (Append-Only File) logs every write operation sequentially, providing much finer-grained durability — down to every second or every command. RDB risks losing minutes of data on crash; AOF risks losing at most one second. Most production deployments enable both: RDB for fast restarts and AOF for durability.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of Redis durability trade-offs and how they affect data loss risk and restart performance.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Assuming Redis is purely in-memory with no persistence, or not knowing that enabling both RDB and AOF is a common and valid production configuration.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention AOF rewrite (BGREWRITEAOF) to compact the AOF file, the appendfsync options (always/everysec/no), and Redis 7's RDB-AOF hybrid format.

sections.title: Fork behavior, restart ordering, and tuning
sections.content:
RDB snapshots rely on `fork()` and copy-on-write: the child writes the snapshot while the parent keeps serving traffic, but a write-heavy dataset can cause COW churn and memory pressure spikes—something to watch when tuning `save` lines. Very large instances sometimes schedule RDB during low-traffic windows or rely on replicas to perform backups so primaries avoid the fork cost.

On restart, when both RDB and AOF exist, Redis prefers loading AOF because it represents the more complete timeline unless you configure otherwise—know this for "what happens after a crash" interview follow-ups. `appendfsync always` minimizes loss but can bottleneck write-heavy apps; `everysec` is the pragmatic default that still bounds loss for most business domains.

Hybrid persistence in Redis 7 combines an RDB preamble with an AOF tail so you get faster restarts than replaying a giant AOF while keeping fine-grained tail durability. Regardless of mode, validate backup restores quarterly: an untested RDB file is just wishful thinking. For pure cache deployments, many teams disable persistence entirely and rely on warm reload from the database, explicitly accepting empty Redis after maintenance—state that choice instead of leaving persistence ambiguous.

One important nuance is the `maxmemory` interaction: if you run both RDB and AOF, the `BGSAVE` fork for snapshots and the `BGREWRITEAOF` fork for compaction can temporarily double memory usage due to copy-on-write pages. Monitor `used_memory_rss` after forks and schedule rewrites during low-traffic windows. Also note that on restart, Redis prefers loading the AOF if it exists because it represents a more complete timeline — which means a corrupted AOF blocks startup unless you run `redis-check-aof --fix`.

sections.title: RDB vs AOF Trade-off Matrix
sections.content:
| Aspect | RDB (Snapshots) | AOF (Append-Only File) |
|---|---|---|
| **Mechanism** | Periodic point-in-time binary snapshot via `BGSAVE` (fork + COW) | Logs every write command as it arrives |
| **Data loss window** | Minutes (since last snapshot) | Seconds (`everysec`) or zero (`always`) |
| **File size** | Compact binary — smaller than AOF | Larger (grows until rewrite); hybrid format in Redis 7 |
| **Restart speed** | Fast — binary load, no replay | Slower — must replay command log (hybrid format mitigates) |
| **CPU impact** | Spike during `fork()`; COW memory pressure on write-heavy instances | Continuous but small; `BGREWRITEAOF` causes periodic fork |
| **Disk I/O** | Burst write during snapshot | Continuous append; `fsync` policy controls throughput |
| **Backup friendliness** | Excellent — single portable file, easy to copy off-host | Possible but file is actively written; prefer RDB for backups |
| **`appendfsync` options** | N/A | `always` (every write), `everysec` (default), `no` (OS decides) |
| **Best for** | Backups, disaster recovery, cold standby bootstrapping | Durability-critical data, minimizing data loss on crash |
| **Production recommendation** | Enable alongside AOF for fast restarts | Enable with `everysec` as the default durability baseline |

sections.title: Redis Configuration for Both Persistence Modes
sections.content:
Redis configuration for enabling both persistence modes:

```bash
# redis.conf — RDB configuration
save 900 1        # Snapshot if ≥1 key changed in 900 seconds
save 300 10       # Snapshot if ≥10 keys changed in 300 seconds
save 60 10000     # Snapshot if ≥10,000 keys changed in 60 seconds
rdbcompression yes
rdbchecksum yes
dbfilename dump.rdb
dir /var/lib/redis

# AOF configuration
appendonly yes
appendfilename "appendonly.aof"
appendfsync everysec               # Best balance of safety and performance
auto-aof-rewrite-percentage 100    # Rewrite when AOF is 2× last rewrite size
auto-aof-rewrite-min-size 64mb     # Don't rewrite tiny AOFs
aof-use-rdb-preamble yes           # Redis 7 hybrid format — fast load + AOF tail

# Memory safety during forks
maxmemory 6gb
maxmemory-policy allkeys-lru
lazyfree-lazy-eviction yes
```

Spring Boot `application.yml` does not configure Redis server persistence directly — these settings live in `redis.conf` on the server. However, you can verify persistence status programmatically:

```java
@Component
public class RedisHealthCheck {

    @Autowired
    private StringRedisTemplate redis;

    public Map<String, String> getPersistenceInfo() {
        Properties info = redis.getConnectionFactory()
            .getConnection().serverCommands().info("persistence");
        return Map.of(
            "rdb_last_save_time", info.getProperty("rdb_last_save_time"),
            "aof_enabled", info.getProperty("aof_enabled"),
            "aof_last_rewrite_status", info.getProperty("aof_last_rewrite_status")
        );
    }
}
```

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **RDB: compact binary snapshot, fast restart, up to interval data loss** — snapshot at intervals; crash between snapshots loses all writes since the last save; best for caches where some data loss is acceptable
- **AOF: every write logged, up to 1s data loss with `everysec` fsync** — replays commands on restart; up to 1s of data loss; larger files and slower restart than RDB
- **`fsync: everysec` is the recommended AOF setting** — 1-second flush window; balances durability and write performance; `fsync: always` is zero-loss but adds latency to every write
- **AOF rewrite compacts the log** — `BGREWRITEAOF` rewrites the file from current state, not full command history; prevents unbounded file growth; configure auto-rewrite thresholds
- **For pure caching: disable persistence** — if the cache can be rebuilt from the database on restart, persistence adds write overhead and complexity without benefit; use `save ""` in redis.conf

sections.title: How to explain this in an interview
sections.content:
Redis is an in-memory store but supports two persistence mechanisms that determine how much data you'd lose on a crash: RDB snapshots and AOF (Append Only File) logging.

**RDB — point-in-time snapshots**
- RDB forks a child process to write the current dataset to a binary snapshot file at configured intervals — `save 900 1` means: save if at least 1 key changed in the last 900 seconds
- Because it's a background fork, RDB snapshots don't block the main Redis process (the fork is fast; the actual write happens in the child)
- The downside is staleness: if Redis crashes between snapshots, all writes since the last snapshot are lost — with a 15-minute interval, you can lose up to 15 minutes of data

**AOF — append-only log of every write command**
- AOF logs every write command to a file in the order it was received — `SET user:1 name Alice`, `EXPIRE user:1 3600` are appended as text; on restart, Redis replays the log to reconstruct the dataset
- AOF with `fsync: everysec` flushes the log to disk every second — at most 1 second of data loss on crash, at the cost of slightly higher write latency
- AOF with `fsync: always` flushes on every write — zero data loss, but much slower; only appropriate for applications with very strict durability requirements

**Combining both**
- The recommended production configuration uses both: AOF for durability (minimal data loss) and RDB for faster restarts — loading a binary snapshot is much faster than replaying millions of AOF commands
- AOF files grow without bound; Redis's AOF rewrite compacts them by rewriting the current state rather than the full command history: `BGREWRITEAOF` or automatic rewrite when the file exceeds a configured size

For caching use cases where the cache can be rebuilt from the database on restart: disable persistence entirely and accept the cache cold-start penalty — it simplifies operations significantly.

questions.question: How do you implement rate limiting in a Spring Boot application using Redis?
questions.title: Rate Limiting with Redis: INCR+EXPIRE and Sliding Window
questions.direct_answer: The simplest Redis rate limiter uses INCR to count requests per time window and EXPIRE to reset the counter, but this fixed-window approach allows bursts at window boundaries. A sliding window log stores request timestamps in a Sorted Set and counts entries in the last N seconds, providing smooth limiting. For production, Lua scripts make these operations atomic, preventing race conditions between INCR and EXPIRE or ZADD and ZREMRANGEBYSCORE.

sections.title: How it works under the hood
sections.content:
Rate limiting protects backend resources from overload by bounding the number of requests a client can make within a time window. Redis is the natural backing store because its atomic operations, sub-millisecond latency, and shared state across application instances make it ideal for enforcing limits in a distributed deployment.

The fixed-window algorithm divides time into discrete buckets. Each bucket is a Redis key whose name encodes the window (e.g., `ratelimit:user42:1705300000`). `INCR` atomically bumps the counter and `EXPIRE` sets the cleanup timer. The critical subtlety is that these two commands must be atomic — if the process crashes between `INCR` (which creates the key implicitly) and `EXPIRE`, the key persists forever and the user is permanently blocked. Wrapping both in a Lua script solves this.

The boundary-burst problem is inherent to fixed windows: a user can exhaust the limit at second 59 of window 1 and again at second 0 of window 2, effectively doubling their rate in a two-second span. The sliding window log fixes this by storing each request's timestamp in a Sorted Set. Before admitting a new request, `ZREMRANGEBYSCORE` drops entries older than the window, the new timestamp is added with `ZADD`, and `ZCARD` counts the remaining entries. Memory scales linearly with the allowed request count per window, so this approach is best suited for moderate limits.

For API gateway-level enforcement, Spring Cloud Gateway ships with a Redis-backed token bucket rate limiter. The token bucket continuously refills at a configurable rate (`replenishRate`) up to a maximum burst size (`burstCapacity`). It handles bursty traffic more gracefully than fixed windows because accumulated tokens absorb short spikes without rejecting requests.

sections.title: Step 1 — Fixed Window with INCR + EXPIRE (Simple)
sections.content:
The simplest rate limiter uses `INCR` with `EXPIRE`, wrapped in a Lua script for atomicity:

```lua
-- rate_limit_fixed.lua
-- KEYS[1] = rate limit key, ARGV[1] = max requests, ARGV[2] = window in seconds
local current = redis.call('INCR', KEYS[1])
if current == 1 then
    redis.call('EXPIRE', KEYS[1], ARGV[2])
end
if current > tonumber(ARGV[1]) then
    return 0  -- rejected
end
return 1      -- allowed
```

**Why Lua?** Without it, a crash between `INCR` (which creates the key implicitly) and `EXPIRE` leaves a counter without a TTL — permanently blocking that client. Lua executes atomically on the Redis server.

**Boundary burst problem:** A user can exhaust the limit at second 59 of window 1, then again at second 0 of window 2, effectively doubling their rate in a 2-second span. The sliding window approach (Step 3) fixes this.

sections.title: Step 2 — Spring Boot Fixed Window Implementation
Step 3 — Sliding Window with Sorted Set
sections.content:
The sliding window stores each request timestamp as a ZSet score, giving smooth rate enforcement:

```lua
-- rate_limit_sliding.lua
-- KEYS[1] = key, ARGV[1] = now (ms), ARGV[2] = window (ms), ARGV[3] = max
local window_start = tonumber(ARGV[1]) - tonumber(ARGV[2])
redis.call('ZREMRANGEBYSCORE', KEYS[1], '-inf', window_start)
local count = redis.call('ZCARD', KEYS[1])
if count >= tonumber(ARGV[3]) then
    return 0  -- rejected
end
redis.call('ZADD', KEYS[1], ARGV[1], ARGV[1] .. ':' .. math.random(100000))
redis.call('EXPIRE', KEYS[1], math.ceil(tonumber(ARGV[2]) / 1000) + 1)
return 1      -- allowed
```

Java integration:

```java
public boolean isAllowedSlidingWindow(String clientId, int maxRequests,
                                       Duration window) {
    String key = "ratelimit:sw:" + clientId;
    long nowMs = Instant.now().toEpochMilli();
    Long result = redis.execute(slidingScript,
        List.of(key),
        String.valueOf(nowMs),
        String.valueOf(window.toMillis()),
        String.valueOf(maxRequests));
    return result != null && result == 1;
}
```

**Trade-off:** Memory scales with the allowed request count (one ZSet entry per request in the window). For limits like 10,000 req/min, consider the fixed-window approach or token bucket instead.

sections.title: Step 4 — Spring Cloud Gateway Built-in Rate Limiter
sections.content:
Spring Cloud Gateway ships with a Redis-backed token bucket rate limiter:

```yaml
# application.yml
spring:
  cloud:
    gateway:
      routes:
        - id: api-route
          uri: http://localhost:8081
          predicates:
            - Path=/api/**
          filters:
            - name: RequestRateLimiter
              args:
                redis-rate-limiter.replenishRate: 10   # 10 tokens/second steady
                redis-rate-limiter.burstCapacity: 20   # Allow burst of 20
                redis-rate-limiter.requestedTokens: 1  # 1 token per request
                key-resolver: "#{@userKeyResolver}"
```

```java
@Bean
public KeyResolver userKeyResolver() {
    // Rate limit by authenticated user, fallback to IP
    return exchange -> Mono.justOrEmpty(
        exchange.getRequest().getHeaders().getFirst("X-User-Id"))
        .switchIfEmpty(Mono.just(
            exchange.getRequest().getRemoteAddress().getAddress().getHostAddress()));
}
```

**How it works:** The gateway uses a Lua script internally that implements the token bucket algorithm. Tokens refill at `replenishRate` per second up to `burstCapacity`. Each request consumes `requestedTokens`. This handles bursty traffic more gracefully than fixed windows — short spikes are absorbed by the bucket's capacity without rejecting requests.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`INCR` with `EXPIRE` is atomic fixed-window rate limiting** — safe under concurrent requests; set the key with `INCR`, then `EXPIRE` on first increment only; `SET key 1 EX 60 NX` sets atomically on creation
- **Fixed window allows boundary bursts** — clients can send the full limit at the end of one window and the full limit at the start of the next; the effective rate in that span is 2x the stated limit
- **Sliding window with Sorted Set eliminates boundary bursts** — score = timestamp; remove old entries with `ZREMRANGEBYSCORE`; count remaining with `ZCARD`; true N-requests-per-window semantics
- **Lua script makes multi-command rate limiting atomic** — `EVAL` executes a Lua script atomically in Redis; the read-check-increment sequence runs as one unit without race conditions between commands
- **Bucket4j with Redis for Spring Boot** — implements token bucket algorithm with Redis persistence; integrates with Spring Cloud Gateway for API-level rate limiting without custom Lua scripts

sections.title: How to explain this in an interview
sections.content:
Rate limiting with Redis is a classic use case because Redis's atomic operations make counter increments safe under concurrent requests from multiple application instances — something in-memory counters can't handle in a distributed deployment.

**Fixed window with INCR**
- The simple approach: `INCR ip:192.168.1.1:2024-01:16:30` increments a counter for this IP in this minute; `EXPIRE` sets the TTL to 60 seconds so the counter resets automatically
- `INCR` is atomic — no two concurrent requests can read and write the counter simultaneously without both their increments being recorded
- The limitation: fixed windows allow bursting at the window boundary — a client can send 100 requests at 11:59 and 100 requests at 12:00, totaling 200 in a 2-second window even though the limit is 100 per minute

**Sliding window with Sorted Set**
- `ZADD requests ip:192.168.1.1 timestamp requestId` adds the request timestamp as the score; `ZREMRANGEBYSCORE` removes entries older than the window; `ZCARD` counts remaining entries
- This gives a true sliding window — the count reflects requests in the last N seconds from now, not from the start of the current minute period; no boundary burst is possible
- Slightly more expensive than INCR: three commands vs one, wrapped in a Lua script for atomicity

**Token bucket with Lua script**
- The most accurate rate limiting model — each client has a bucket of tokens that refills at a fixed rate; each request consumes one token; if the bucket is empty, the request is rejected
- Implement in a Lua script (`EVAL`) to make the read-compute-write atomic in Redis; or use the Bucket4j library which integrates with Redis for Spring Boot applications

Bucket4j with a Redis backend is the recommended production approach for Spring Boot — it provides token bucket semantics, configures via Spring Cloud Gateway, and handles the Lua atomicity automatically.

questions.question: When would you use Redis pub/sub versus Apache Kafka for messaging, and what are the key trade-offs?
questions.title: Redis Pub/Sub vs Apache Kafka
questions.direct_answer: Redis pub/sub is a fire-and-forget broadcast mechanism with no message persistence, no consumer groups, and no offset tracking — messages sent while a subscriber is offline are lost. Kafka is a distributed commit log with durable storage, consumer group semantics, replay capability, and high-throughput ordering guarantees. Use Redis pub/sub for ephemeral real-time events like WebSocket fan-out or cache invalidation; use Kafka for event sourcing, audit logs, inter-service messaging, or anywhere message delivery guarantees matter.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of message durability, delivery guarantees, and the operational complexity trade-off between Redis and Kafka.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Treating Redis pub/sub as a reliable message queue — it has no persistence and messages are dropped if no subscriber is connected.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention Redis Streams as a middle ground: they have Kafka-like consumer groups and message persistence while being simpler to operate than Kafka, and are built into Redis.

sections.title: Messaging paradigms: fire-and-forget vs durable log
sections.content:
Redis pub/sub and Apache Kafka represent opposite ends of the messaging durability spectrum, and choosing between them is one of the most common architecture decisions in distributed Java systems.

Redis pub/sub operates as a stateless broadcast channel. When a publisher sends a message to a channel, Redis immediately delivers it to every currently connected subscriber and then discards it — there is no buffer, no log, no acknowledgment. If a subscriber disconnects for even a moment, messages published during that window are permanently lost. This makes pub/sub ideal for ephemeral signals: cache invalidation broadcasts, real-time WebSocket fan-out, and typing indicators in chat applications where losing an occasional message is harmless.

Kafka, by contrast, is a distributed commit log. Every message is appended to a durable, partitioned log and retained for a configurable period (hours, days, or indefinitely with compaction). Consumers maintain an offset into the log and can replay from any point — making Kafka suitable for event sourcing, audit trails, analytics pipelines, and inter-service communication where message loss is unacceptable. Consumer groups enable parallel processing: Kafka assigns partitions to consumers within a group so each message is processed by exactly one consumer, with automatic rebalancing on failure.

Redis Streams, introduced in Redis 5, sit between these two extremes. Streams store messages durably in Redis memory (or on disk via persistence), support consumer groups with `XREADGROUP` and acknowledgment via `XACK`, and allow replay by message ID. They lack Kafka's partition-level parallelism and cross-datacenter replication, but for moderate-scale event logs (thousands to low millions of messages per second), Streams eliminate the operational overhead of running a separate Kafka cluster. The decision framework is: pub/sub for fire-and-forget broadcast, Streams for durable in-Redis event logs, and Kafka when you need proven scalability, exactly-once semantics, or multi-datacenter replication.

sections.title: Redis Pub/Sub vs Kafka vs Redis Streams
sections.content:
| Aspect | Redis Pub/Sub | Apache Kafka | Redis Streams |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Durability** | None — fire and forget | Durable commit log with configurable retention | Durable in Redis memory (+ RDB/AOF) |
| **Delivery guarantee** | At-most-once | At-least-once / exactly-once (with transactions) | At-least-once (with XACK) |
| **Consumer groups** | No — all subscribers get all messages | Yes — partitions assigned to group members | Yes — `XREADGROUP` + `XACK` |
| **Message replay** | Not possible — messages discarded after delivery | Full replay from any offset | Replay by message ID |
| **Ordering** | Per channel | Per partition (partition-key ordering) | Global within a single stream |
| **Throughput** | ~1M msg/sec (simple broadcast) | Millions msg/sec (partitioned, batched) | ~100K–500K msg/sec per stream |
| **Backpressure** | None — slow subscribers are disconnected | Consumer controls read pace via offset | Consumer controls via `COUNT` + `BLOCK` |
| **Offline consumers** | Messages lost | Messages retained until retention expires | Messages retained until trimmed |
| **Operational complexity** | Zero — built into Redis | High — ZooKeeper/KRaft, brokers, schema registry | Low — built into Redis |
| **Best for** | Cache invalidation, live notifications, typing indicators | Event sourcing, audit logs, inter-service messaging, analytics | Moderate-scale event logs, task queues within Redis |

Key Points
sections.content:
- **Redis pub/sub is fire-and-forget** — no persistence; if no subscriber is connected at publish time, the message is lost; appropriate only when losing messages is acceptable
- **Kafka is durable and replayable** — messages stored on disk; consumers track offset; restart and replay from where you left off; at-least-once delivery is guaranteed
- **Redis pub/sub for cache invalidation and real-time dashboards** — low latency broadcast; no delivery guarantee needed; appropriate when the client can refresh on reconnect
- **Kafka for event sourcing, audit trails, multi-consumer fan-out** — multiple independent consumer groups each see all events; order within a partition is guaranteed; replayable for backfill
- **Redis Streams as the middle ground** — persistent ordered log with consumer groups and acknowledgment; lower operational complexity than Kafka; appropriate for moderate-throughput reliable messaging on an existing Redis instance

sections.title: How to explain this in an interview
sections.content:
Redis pub/sub and Kafka both enable event-driven communication between services, but they have fundamentally different delivery guarantees — choosing the wrong one is a common architecture mistake.

**Redis pub/sub — fire and forget**
- Redis pub/sub is a broadcast channel: `PUBLISH channel message` sends to all current subscribers; if no subscriber is connected when the publish happens, the message is gone — there's no persistence, no replay, no offset tracking
- This makes it appropriate for: cache invalidation events, real-time dashboards where missing a few updates doesn't matter, broadcasting session logout to all app instances, live notification delivery where the client can refresh on reconnect
- `SUBSCRIBE` and `PSUBSCRIBE` (pattern-based) are the consumer commands; the subscriber must be connected at publish time to receive the message

**Kafka — durable, ordered, replayable**
- Kafka stores messages on disk in an ordered log partitioned across brokers — consumers can replay from any offset, which means a restarted consumer can pick up where it left off without losing messages
- Consumer groups allow multiple consumers to share the processing load; each partition is assigned to one consumer in the group; messages are redelivered until acknowledged
- Kafka is the right choice when: messages must be processed at least once even after consumer restarts; order within a partition matters; multiple independent consumer groups need to process the same events; the system needs replay capability for debugging or backfill

**Redis Streams — the middle ground**
- Redis Streams add persistence and consumer group semantics to Redis — messages are stored in an ordered log, consumers acknowledge processing, and unacknowledged messages can be reclaimed; much simpler to operate than Kafka for lower-throughput use cases
- For a single Redis instance use case where losing some messages is acceptable but consumer groups and delivery acknowledgment are needed, Streams is the right choice over raw pub/sub

questions.question: What is the cache stampede (thundering herd) problem and how do you prevent it in a Spring Boot application?
questions.title: Cache Stampede (Thundering Herd) Problem and Solutions
questions.direct_answer: A cache stampede occurs when a popular cache entry expires and many concurrent requests all miss simultaneously, each triggering an expensive database or downstream service call at the same time, potentially overwhelming the backend. Solutions include probabilistic early expiration (PER), distributed locking to ensure only one request refreshes the cache while others wait or serve stale data, and background refresh patterns where the cache is populated asynchronously before expiry.

interviewer_intent.testing: Awareness of cache failure modes under load and practical mitigation strategies, not just knowing what the problem is called.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Proposing 'just set a longer TTL' as the solution — this reduces frequency but does not eliminate the stampede when the TTL eventually expires.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the probabilistic early expiration algorithm's formula and discuss serving stale-while-revalidate as an HTTP-inspired pattern applicable to Redis.

sections.title: How it works under the hood
sections.content:
The cache stampede is a cascading failure pattern that emerges under high concurrency when a popular cache entry expires simultaneously for many requesters. Unlike a simple cache miss — which adds one database round-trip — a stampede multiplies the miss by the concurrency level, sending hundreds or thousands of identical queries to a database that was never provisioned for that load.

The root cause is a lack of coordination: every thread independently detects the miss and independently decides to refresh. The mutex (single-flight) pattern fixes this by acquiring a distributed lock before querying the database. The first thread to acquire the lock performs the refresh; all others either block waiting for the lock (and then re-check the cache) or return a stale value if one is available. The double-check after acquiring the lock is essential — by the time the second thread wins the lock, the first may have already repopulated the cache.

Probabilistic early expiration (PER) takes a statistical approach. Each request evaluates a formula based on the remaining TTL and a random draw: as the TTL approaches zero, the probability of triggering an early refresh increases. This spreads the refresh workload across time and across different request threads, so no single expiry cliff exists. The algorithm is tuned by a beta parameter that controls how aggressively refreshes are pulled forward.

The stale-while-revalidate pattern, borrowed from HTTP cache semantics, returns the expired value immediately to keep latency low and kicks off an asynchronous background task to refresh the cache. This is particularly effective for read-heavy services where a few seconds of staleness is acceptable and user-perceived latency is the primary concern. In Spring, setting `@Cacheable(sync = true)` provides a built-in mutex that synchronizes cache population per key, offering basic stampede protection without custom locking code.

sections.title: The Problem
sections.content: At T=0, a cache entry for a hot product page (served 10,000 req/s) expires. All 10,000 in-flight requests miss the cache simultaneously. Each request independently queries the database, which is sized for a handful of concurrent queries, not 10,000. The database buckles under load, requests time out, the cache is never repopulated, and the system enters a failure cascade.

sections.title: Vulnerable Implementation
Root Cause Analysis
sections.content:
**Why does the stampede happen?**

1. **Simultaneous expiry:** All 10,000 concurrent requests were being served from a single cache entry. When it expires, all 10,000 threads discover the miss within milliseconds of each other.

2. **No coordination:** Each thread independently decides to refresh the cache. There is no "someone else is already handling this" signal.

3. **Amplification:** The database receives 10,000 identical queries instead of 1. If the query takes 50ms, the database suddenly has 10,000 × 50ms = 500 seconds of work queued.

4. **Cascade failure:** Database connection pool exhausts → requests queue → timeouts → the cache is never repopulated → more requests hit the database → system spirals.

**The fundamental issue is a lack of mutual exclusion on cache population.** The cache expiry creates a critical section (load from DB → write to cache) that must be executed by exactly one thread.

sections.title: Solution 1 — Distributed Lock (Mutex Refresh)
Solution 2 — Probabilistic Early Expiration (PER)
Key Points
sections.content:
- **Stampede occurs when a popular entry expires under high concurrency** — all concurrent requests miss simultaneously, all hit the database, all write the same key; the database receives the full request rate at once
- **Mutex lock (Redis `SET NX`) gates database access to one caller** — first caller fills the cache; others wait; prevents N simultaneous database queries for the same key; lock TTL must exceed the database query time
- **Probabilistic early expiry prevents synchronized expiry** — requests proactively refresh with increasing probability as TTL decreases; the cache is refreshed before expiry, so no synchronized miss occurs
- **Background refresh keeps the cache perpetually warm** — a scheduled job refreshes TTL before expiry; user requests never see a cache miss for hot keys; the database is queried once per TTL period
- **Jitter on TTLs reduces synchronized expiry across keys** — if many keys expire at the same time (e.g., all set at application startup with the same TTL), they all stampede together; add random jitter to the TTL on cache set

sections.title: How to explain this in an interview
sections.content:
A cache stampede happens when a popular cache entry expires and many concurrent requests all miss simultaneously, all hit the database, and all try to write the same key back to the cache. At scale, this can take a database from healthy to overloaded in seconds.

**Why it happens**
- Under normal load, the cache handles thousands of requests per second for a popular entry; when that entry expires, all those requests reach the database at the same moment — which means the database receives the full request rate for that entry directly, rather than a trickle of cache misses
- The database query may be expensive (joining three tables, aggregating millions of rows), so every concurrent thread runs it simultaneously; the database can't handle that load, latency spikes, and the storm persists until the cache is repopulated

**Mutex locking — one filler, others wait**
- Use Redis's `SET key NX EX 10` as a distributed mutex — only the first caller to acquire it queries the database and fills the cache; all other concurrent callers wait briefly and then read from the populated cache
- The downside: callers that fail to acquire the lock must wait; if the database query is slow, they wait for the full query duration; implementation must handle the case where the lock holder fails before filling the cache

**Probabilistic early expiry**
- Rather than expiring all at once, each request has a small probability of re-fetching early based on the remaining TTL — requests start proactively refreshing the cache before it expires, so expiry never causes a synchronized miss
- The algorithm: as TTL decreases, the probability of early refresh increases; by the time the cache actually expires, the value has already been refreshed by a lucky early request

**Background refresh — never expose expiry to requests**
- A background thread monitors cache TTLs and proactively refreshes entries before they expire — user-facing requests always hit a warm cache because expiry happens in the background, not in the request path
- This is the cleanest solution for high-traffic hot keys: the cache is always warm, and the database query runs once per TTL period regardless of traffic volume

questions.question: What is the difference between Redis Cluster and Redis Sentinel, and when do you use each?
questions.title: Redis Cluster vs Redis Sentinel: High Availability and Horizontal Scaling
questions.direct_answer: Redis Sentinel provides high availability for a single Redis dataset through automatic failover: it monitors a primary and replicas, promoting a replica if the primary fails. Redis Cluster provides both high availability and horizontal scaling by sharding the keyspace across multiple primary nodes (each with its own replicas), supporting datasets larger than a single node's memory and distributing read/write load. Use Sentinel when one node has enough capacity; use Cluster when you need to scale beyond a single node.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of the architectural difference between HA-only vs HA-plus-sharding, and awareness of Cluster's limitations like multi-key operation restrictions.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking Sentinel provides sharding or that Cluster replaces Sentinel — Cluster has its own built-in failover, so you do not need Sentinel with Cluster.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that Redis Cluster uses consistent hashing with 16,384 hash slots, discuss the limitations of multi-key operations (keys must be in the same slot unless using hash tags), and mention that Spring Data Redis supports both via LettuceConnectionFactory.

sections.title: High availability vs horizontal scaling in Redis
sections.content:
Redis Sentinel and Redis Cluster solve overlapping but distinct problems, and conflating them is a common interview mistake. Understanding when each is appropriate requires grasping the architectural difference between high availability (keeping a single dataset available during node failures) and horizontal scaling (distributing a dataset across multiple nodes to exceed single-node capacity).

Sentinel is a set of monitoring processes that run alongside your Redis deployment. It continuously health-checks the primary, and when a quorum of Sentinel instances agrees the primary is unreachable, it promotes one of the replicas to primary and reconfigures the remaining replicas to follow the new primary. The application connects via Sentinel-aware clients (like Lettuce in Spring) that query Sentinel for the current primary address and reconnect automatically after failover. The dataset itself remains bounded by a single primary's memory — Sentinel provides no sharding.

Redis Cluster shards the 16,384-slot keyspace across multiple primary nodes, each with its own set of replicas. When a primary fails, its replicas participate in an election and the winner takes over the failed primary's hash slots — no external Sentinel process is needed. The total dataset capacity equals the sum of all primaries' memory, and write throughput scales with the number of shards. However, multi-key commands (`MGET`, `MSET`, `SUNION`) only work when all involved keys hash to the same slot, because a single command cannot span nodes. Redis addresses this with hash tags: wrapping a substring in curly braces (`{user:42}:profile`) forces Redis to hash only the tagged portion, co-locating related keys on the same shard.

In Spring Data Redis, the switch between modes is a configuration change: `RedisSentinelConfiguration` vs `RedisClusterConfiguration` on the `LettuceConnectionFactory`. Application code using `RedisTemplate` or `@Cacheable` remains unchanged, though Cluster deployments must be aware of the hash-slot constraint when designing key schemas.

sections.title: Sentinel vs Cluster Trade-offs
sections.content:
| Aspect | Redis Sentinel | Redis Cluster |
|---|---|---|
| **Purpose** | High availability (automatic failover) | HA + horizontal scaling (sharding) |
| **Data distribution** | Single primary holds entire dataset | Sharded across N primaries via 16,384 hash slots |
| **Max dataset size** | Limited to one node's RAM | Sum of all primary nodes' RAM |
| **Write throughput** | Single primary bottleneck | Scales with number of primaries |
| **Failover mechanism** | External Sentinel processes monitor + promote | Built-in: replicas elect a new primary per shard |
| **Multi-key operations** | Full support (single node) | Only if all keys hash to the same slot (use hash tags) |
| **Lua scripts** | Full access to all keys | Keys must be in the same slot |
| **Transactions (MULTI)** | Full support | Same-slot keys only |
| **Client complexity** | Sentinel-aware client queries master address | Cluster-aware client handles MOVED/ASK redirections |
| **Minimum nodes** | 1 primary + 1 replica + 3 Sentinels | 3 primaries + 3 replicas (6 nodes minimum) |
| **Spring config** | `spring.data.redis.sentinel.*` | `spring.data.redis.cluster.*` |
| **Operational complexity** | Low — familiar primary-replica model | Medium — resharding, slot migration, redirect handling |
| **Best for** | Datasets < 50 GB, single-primary workloads | Large datasets, write-heavy workloads needing horizontal scale |

sections.title: Spring Boot Configuration for Both
sections.content:
Spring Boot configuration for Sentinel and Cluster:

**Sentinel configuration (`application.yml`):**
```yaml
spring:
  data:
    redis:
      sentinel:
        master: mymaster
        nodes:
          - sentinel-1:26379
          - sentinel-2:26379
          - sentinel-3:26379
      password: ${REDIS_PASSWORD}
      lettuce:
        pool:
          max-active: 16
```

**Cluster configuration (`application.yml`):**
```yaml
spring:
  data:
    redis:
      cluster:
        nodes:
          - redis-1:6379
          - redis-2:6379
          - redis-3:6379
          - redis-4:6379
          - redis-5:6379
          - redis-6:6379
        max-redirects: 3   # Max MOVED/ASK redirections per command
      password: ${REDIS_PASSWORD}
      lettuce:
        pool:
          max-active: 16
```

Both modes use the same `LettuceConnectionFactory` — your `RedisTemplate` and `@Cacheable` code does not change. The Lettuce driver handles Sentinel master discovery and Cluster slot routing transparently.

```java
// Hash tags force related keys to the same Cluster slot
String profileKey = "{user:42}:profile";
String settingsKey = "{user:42}:settings";
// Both keys hash on "user:42" → guaranteed same slot → MGET works
redisTemplate.opsForValue().multiGet(List.of(profileKey, settingsKey));
```

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Sentinel: HA for a single dataset** — automatic failover without partitioning; all data on one primary + replicas; requires three Sentinel processes for quorum; dataset limited to one node's RAM
- **Cluster: partitioned dataset + HA** — 16,384 hash slots distributed across N primaries; each primary has replicas; dataset grows with node count; total capacity exceeds one node's RAM
- **Cluster restricts multi-key commands** — `MGET`, `SUNIONSTORE` only work when all keys are in the same hash slot; use `{hashtag}` notation in key names to force co-location of related keys
- **Sentinel is simpler for most applications** — if the dataset fits in one node's RAM, Sentinel provides failover without the operational complexity of hash slot management and cross-slot restrictions
- **Spring Boot configuration** — `spring.redis.sentinel.*` for Sentinel mode; `spring.redis.cluster.nodes` for Cluster; Lettuce (the default Redis client) supports both transparently

sections.title: How to explain this in an interview
sections.content:
Redis Sentinel and Redis Cluster solve different problems. Sentinel provides high availability for a single dataset; Cluster provides both high availability and horizontal data partitioning across multiple nodes.

**Redis Sentinel — HA for a single dataset**
- Sentinel monitors a primary-replica set and performs automatic failover — if the primary becomes unreachable, Sentinel promotes the replica with the most current data and updates clients about the new primary address
- Sentinel itself runs on separate processes (typically three) to avoid a single point of failure in the monitoring layer; a majority of Sentinels must agree before promoting a replica
- All data lives on one primary (plus replicas) — Sentinel doesn't partition data, it just ensures the primary is always available; dataset size is limited by one node's RAM

**Redis Cluster — data partitioned across N primaries**
- Cluster splits the keyspace into 16,384 hash slots and distributes them across multiple primary nodes — which means the total dataset size can exceed one node's RAM because different keys live on different nodes
- Each primary has its own replica(s) for failover within its slot range — losing a primary promotes its replica automatically without external Sentinel processes
- Cluster introduces key restrictions: multi-key commands (`MGET`, `SUNIONSTORE`) only work when all keys map to the same hash slot; use `{hashtag}` in key names to force co-location of related keys

**Which to choose**
- Use Sentinel when your dataset fits on one Redis instance but you need failover — the operational simplicity is significant and most Spring Boot applications don't need to partition their Redis data
- Use Cluster when your dataset is too large for one node's RAM, or write throughput exceeds what one primary can handle
- In Spring Boot: configure `spring.redis.sentinel.master` and `spring.redis.sentinel.nodes` for Sentinel; `spring.redis.cluster.nodes` for Cluster
