questions.question: What are the main cache invalidation strategies and how do you implement them in Spring Boot with Redis?
questions.title: Cache Invalidation Strategies in Spring Boot with Redis
questions.direct_answer: Cache invalidation strategies include TTL-based expiry (entries expire automatically after a fixed duration), event-driven invalidation (write operations evict or update specific cache keys), pattern-based bulk eviction (delete all keys matching a prefix), and publish/subscribe invalidation (broadcast eviction commands to all application nodes sharing a distributed cache). Spring's @CacheEvict handles explicit invalidation, but complex invalidation patterns often require direct RedisTemplate usage or a Redis pub/sub broadcast.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical knowledge of cache consistency strategies beyond simple TTLs, especially for distributed systems where multiple app instances share a Redis cache.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Relying solely on TTL for consistency without handling write-triggered invalidation, resulting in stale data for the full TTL duration after an update.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Discuss the two hard problems of computer science joke, then seriously cover versioned cache keys as an alternative to explicit invalidation, and mention cache-tag-based invalidation used by CDNs and frameworks like Symfony.

sections.title: Why cache invalidation is hard — and how to manage it
sections.content:
Phil Karlton's famous quip — 'there are only two hard things in computer science: cache invalidation and naming things' — resonates because invalidation sits at the intersection of consistency, performance, and operational complexity. Every invalidation strategy trades one of these for another.

TTL-based expiry is the simplest: every entry gets an `EXPIRE` and Redis automatically evicts it after the timer elapses. The staleness window equals the TTL — a 10-minute TTL means users may see data up to 10 minutes out of date. This is acceptable for product catalogs, feature flags, or configuration, but unacceptable for user balances or inventory counts. Even when you use event-driven invalidation, always set a TTL as a safety net so orphaned keys (from bugs or missed events) eventually clean up.

Event-driven invalidation ties cache eviction to write operations. When a `User` entity is updated, the service explicitly evicts `users:42` from Redis. Spring's `@CacheEvict` automates this declaratively. The challenge is cascading invalidation: updating a `Category` might affect thousands of `Product` cache entries. Pattern-based eviction (`SCAN` + `DEL` for matching keys) handles this but is expensive on large keyspaces. Avoid `KEYS *` in production — it blocks the single-threaded Redis command loop for the entire scan duration.

For multi-level caching (Caffeine in front of Redis), a single instance evicting from Redis does not clear other instances' local caches. Redis pub/sub broadcast invalidation solves this: the writing instance publishes an invalidation message, and all instances subscribe and evict from their local caches. Versioned cache keys offer an alternative: encode a generation counter in the key (`product:42:v7`), bump the version on write, and let old entries expire via TTL — no explicit invalidation needed.

sections.title: Four Cache Invalidation Strategies
sections.content:
**Strategy 1 — TTL-Based Expiry (Passive)**
Every cached entry gets a time-to-live. Redis automatically removes it when the timer elapses. Staleness window equals the TTL. Best as a safety net under all other strategies.

**Strategy 2 — Event-Driven Invalidation (Active)**
Write operations explicitly evict or update specific cache keys. Spring's `@CacheEvict` handles this declaratively. Challenge: cascading invalidation when one write affects many cached entries.

**Strategy 3 — Versioned Cache Keys**
Encode a generation counter in the key: `product:42:v7`. On write, increment the version. Old entries become unreachable and expire via TTL. No explicit invalidation logic needed.

**Strategy 4 — Pub/Sub Broadcast Invalidation**
For multi-level caches (Caffeine + Redis), the writing instance publishes an invalidation event on a Redis channel. All instances subscribe and evict from their local caches. Essential when local in-process caches front the shared Redis cache.

| Strategy | Staleness | Complexity | Best For |
|---|---|---|---|
| TTL-only | Up to TTL duration | Lowest | Config data, feature flags |
| Event-driven (`@CacheEvict`) | Near-zero | Low-medium | User profiles, product data |
| Versioned keys | Near-zero | Medium | High-cardinality entities |
| Pub/Sub broadcast | Near-zero (cross-instance) | Medium-high | Multi-level cache architectures |

Key Points
sections.content:
- **TTL is the simplest invalidation** — entries expire automatically; appropriate when a small staleness window is acceptable; every cache entry should have a TTL even when other invalidation is used as a safety net
- **`@CacheEvict` on write for immediate consistency** — delete the cache key in the same service method that writes to the database; the next read re-fetches fresh data and repopulates the cache
- **TTL as backup even with event-driven invalidation** — if the eviction call fails (Redis unavailable, exception before eviction runs), the TTL ensures the stale entry eventually expires; never rely on eviction alone

sections.title: How to explain this in an interview
sections.content:
Cache invalidation is the hard part of caching — knowing when a cached value is stale and needs to be refreshed. The three main strategies are TTL-based expiry, event-driven invalidation, and versioned keys.

**TTL — simplest, always slightly stale**
- Set a time-to-live on every cache entry — `SET key value EX 300` expires after 5 minutes regardless of whether the underlying data changed
- TTL is appropriate when some staleness is acceptable: product catalog, configuration settings, reference data that changes infrequently; the application tolerate serving data that's up to 5 minutes old
- The downside: a record updated 10 seconds after caching will serve the old value for the remaining TTL; for writes that must be visible immediately, TTL alone is insufficient

**Event-driven invalidation — immediate consistency**
- When a record is updated, explicitly delete or update the corresponding cache key — `@CacheEvict` in Spring, or a manual `redisTemplate.delete(key)` call in the service method that performs the write
- This is the correct pattern when reads must reflect the latest write promptly — a user updates their profile and the next page load must show the change, not the cached version
- The risk: if the write succeeds but the cache eviction fails (Redis is temporarily unavailable), the cache remains stale; use cache eviction as a best-effort operation, relying on a backup TTL to eventually expire the stale entry

**Versioned keys — invalidate by changing the key**
- Instead of evicting a key, change the version portion of the key — `product:v2:123` replaces `product:v1:123` after an update; the old key is never explicitly deleted, it just stops being referenced and expires via TTL
- Useful for bulk invalidation: incrementing a global version prefix invalidates all cache entries of that type without needing to know which specific keys to evict

questions.question: How do you configure Spring Session with Redis to enable distributed session storage in a multi-instance Spring Boot application?
questions.title: Spring Session + Redis for Distributed Session Storage
questions.direct_answer: Spring Session replaces the default in-memory HttpSession with a Redis-backed session store, enabling any application instance to serve any request regardless of which instance created the session. You add spring-session-data-redis to your dependencies, annotate a configuration class with @EnableRedisHttpSession, and configure a Redis connection — Spring's autoconfiguration handles the rest. Session data is stored as a Redis Hash, and the session ID is passed via a cookie or HTTP header.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of the stateless application pattern, sticky session problems, and how Redis-backed sessions enable horizontal scaling.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using Spring Session without setting appropriate session timeouts, leading to Redis being filled with abandoned sessions that consume significant memory.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention the difference between cookie-based and header-based session ID propagation, discuss session data serialization concerns, and explain how Spring Session supports multiple session repositories (Redis, JDBC, Hazelcast).

sections.title: How it works under the hood
sections.content:
HTTP session management becomes a distributed systems problem the moment you scale beyond a single application instance. With in-memory sessions, each JVM holds its own session map, so the load balancer must route every request from a given user to the same instance (sticky sessions). This creates uneven load distribution, complicates rolling deployments, and means a single instance failure loses all its active sessions.

Spring Session solves this by replacing the servlet container's default `HttpSession` implementation with a pluggable `SessionRepository`. The Redis implementation stores each session as a Redis Hash under a namespaced key (e.g., `spring:session:sessions:<uuid>`), with each session attribute serialized as a Hash field. A separate Redis key with an expiry tracks the session's max inactive interval, and Spring Session uses Redis keyspace notifications to detect expired sessions and fire `SessionDestroyedEvent` to application listeners.

The flush mode setting controls write timing. `ON_SAVE` (default) buffers attribute changes in memory and flushes to Redis only when the HTTP response is committed — this batches writes and reduces Redis round-trips but risks data loss if the JVM crashes mid-request. `IMMEDIATE` mode writes every `setAttribute` call to Redis synchronously, which is safer for long-running requests or WebSocket connections where the response is never formally committed.

Serialization deserves attention: every object stored in the session must be serializable. JDK serialization works out of the box but produces verbose payloads and is fragile across class version changes. Switching to JSON serialization (via Jackson) produces human-readable Redis entries and avoids `ClassNotFoundException` during rolling deployments, but requires careful handling of polymorphic types. Keep session payloads small — large session objects inflate Redis memory and add latency to every request that touches the session.

sections.title: Step 1 — Add Dependencies
sections.content:
Add Spring Session and Redis dependencies:

```xml
<!-- pom.xml -->
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.session</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-session-data-redis</artifactId>
</dependency>
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-data-redis</artifactId>
</dependency>
```

Spring Boot auto-configures Spring Session when it detects the `spring-session-data-redis` dependency on the classpath. No additional code is needed for the basic setup.

sections.title: Step 2 — Enable Redis HTTP Session
Step 3 — Configure Redis and Session in application.yml
sections.content:
```yaml
# application.yml
spring:
  data:
    redis:
      host: ${REDIS_HOST:localhost}
      port: ${REDIS_PORT:6379}
      password: ${REDIS_PASSWORD:}
      lettuce:
        pool:
          max-active: 16
          max-idle: 8
          min-idle: 2

  session:
    store-type: redis              # Explicitly select Redis
    timeout: 30m                   # Max inactive interval
    redis:
      namespace: myapp:session     # Key prefix
      flush-mode: on-save          # or "immediate" for WebSocket/SSE

server:
  servlet:
    session:
      cookie:
        name: SESSIONID
        http-only: true
        secure: true
        max-age: -1                # Session cookie (expires on browser close)
```

**Redis key structure** created by Spring Session:
- `myapp:session:sessions:<uuid>` — Hash containing session attributes
- `myapp:session:expirations:<timestamp>` — Set of session IDs expiring at that time
- `myapp:session:sessions:expires:<uuid>` — Phantom key for keyspace notification on expiry

sections.title: How to explain this in an interview
sections.content:
Spring Session replaces the default in-memory `HttpSession` with a Redis-backed session store, enabling horizontal scaling without sticky sessions.

**The problem it solves**
- By default, Spring Boot stores sessions in application memory — which means if a load balancer routes a user's second request to a different app instance, that instance has no record of the session, and the user appears logged out
- The traditional fix is sticky sessions (session affinity): the load balancer pins each user to one instance; the problem is that instance failures lose all sessions on that node, and load distribution becomes uneven as instances have different session loads
- Spring Session externalizes the session to Redis: every instance reads from and writes to the same Redis store, which means any instance can handle any request for any user

**Configuration in Spring Boot**
- Add `spring-boot-starter-data-redis` and `spring-session-data-redis`; the session store is auto-configured; configure timeout with `server.servlet.session.timeout`
- Spring Session serializes the session to a Redis Hash under `spring:session:sessions:{sessionId}` — each session attribute is a Hash field; reading one attribute doesn't deserialize the entire session

**Session clustering considerations**
- Redis for sessions introduces a network round trip on every request — typically fast (sub-millisecond on the same network), but it's worth measuring; use connection pooling to avoid connection overhead
- `@SessionScope` beans work correctly with Spring Session — the session bean's lifecycle is tied to the Redis-backed session, not the application instance
- Configure session serialization carefully: the default Java serialization can cause ClassNotFoundException after a deployment if serialized classes change; use JSON serialization with a consistent schema

questions.title: Redis Memory Optimization: Eviction Policies and maxmemory Configuration
questions.direct_answer: Redis memory optimization combines the right eviction policy, appropriate data structure choices, key expiry discipline, and maxmemory limits. The eviction policy determines what Redis does when it hits its memory limit — allkeys-lru evicts the least-recently-used key regardless of TTL, while volatile-lru only evicts keys that have a TTL set. For a cache-only Redis, allkeys-lru is the standard choice; for a mixed cache and persistent data store, volatile-lru protects keys without TTLs from eviction.

interviewer_intent.testing: Operational awareness of Redis memory management, eviction policies, and the implications of hitting maxmemory for application behavior.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not setting maxmemory at all, allowing Redis to consume all available RAM and trigger OOM kills, or using the default noeviction policy with a cache workload.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention Redis's memory encoding optimizations (ziplist/listpack for small collections), the OBJECT ENCODING command to inspect encodings, and Redis 7's listpack replacing ziplist.

sections.title: Memory management: the operational backbone of production Redis
sections.content:
Redis stores everything in RAM, so memory management is not optional — it is the most critical operational concern. Without a `maxmemory` setting, Redis will consume all available RAM until the operating system's OOM killer terminates the process, causing an unplanned outage. Setting `maxmemory` to 70–80% of available RAM leaves headroom for the OS page cache, replication buffers, and the memory overhead of `BGSAVE`/`BGREWRITEAOF` forks (which can temporarily double memory usage via copy-on-write).

The eviction policy determines what happens when Redis hits the memory ceiling. The default `noeviction` policy returns an error on write commands, which is appropriate for session stores or queues where silent data loss is unacceptable. For pure caches, `allkeys-lru` is the standard: it evicts the least recently used key from the entire keyspace. `allkeys-lfu` (least frequently used) performs better under power-law access distributions where a small set of hot keys should never be evicted despite being accessed less recently than a burst of cold keys. `volatile-lru` and `volatile-lfu` restrict eviction to keys that have a TTL set, which is useful when Redis serves as both a cache (keys with TTL) and a persistent store (keys without TTL).

Beyond eviction policy, data structure choice is the biggest memory lever. Redis uses compact internal encodings — listpack (replacing ziplist in Redis 7) — for small Hashes, Lists, Sets, and ZSets. A Hash with fewer than `hash-max-listpack-entries` (128 by default) fields uses a flat array that consumes roughly 10× less memory than a full hash table. Storing a user's attributes as one Hash instead of N separate String keys saves both the per-key overhead (~70 bytes each) and enables the compact encoding. Monitoring `OBJECT ENCODING <key>` and `MEMORY USAGE <key>` helps identify keys that have outgrown their compact encoding.

Serialization format also matters: JDK serialization stores class metadata and is 2–3× larger than JSON, which is in turn larger than binary formats like Protobuf or Kryo. For high-cardinality caches, switching serializers can reduce Redis memory by 30–50%. Combine compact serialization with short key names (abbreviate when key count is in the millions) and mandatory TTLs on every key to keep memory predictable.

sections.title: Eviction Policies Explained
sections.content:
Redis offers 8 eviction policies, grouped by scope:

**All-keys policies** (operate on the entire keyspace):
- **`allkeys-lru`** — Evicts the least recently used key. Best for general-purpose caching where you want hot data retained.
- **`allkeys-lfu`** — Evicts the least frequently used key. Better than LRU when access follows a power-law distribution (few very hot keys).
- **`allkeys-random`** — Evicts a random key. Fast but unpredictable — rarely the right choice.

**Volatile policies** (only evict keys with a TTL set):
- **`volatile-lru`** — LRU among keys with `EXPIRE`. Protects keys without TTL from eviction.
- **`volatile-lfu`** — LFU among keys with `EXPIRE`.
- **`volatile-random`** — Random eviction among keys with `EXPIRE`.
- **`volatile-ttl`** — Evicts the key closest to expiration. Useful when short-TTL keys are least valuable.

**No eviction:**
- **`noeviction`** (default) — Returns an error on writes when `maxmemory` is reached. Appropriate for session stores or queues where silent data loss is unacceptable.

**Decision framework:**
- Pure cache → `allkeys-lru` or `allkeys-lfu`
- Mixed cache + persistent data → `volatile-lru` (protects persistent keys)
- Session store → `noeviction` (fail loudly, don't lose sessions)
- Short-lived data → `volatile-ttl` (evict nearest-to-expire first)

sections.title: Redis Memory Configuration
sections.content:
```bash
# redis.conf — Memory management
maxmemory 6gb                       # 70-80% of available RAM
maxmemory-policy allkeys-lru        # Evict least recently used
maxmemory-samples 10                # Sample size for LRU approximation (default 5)

# Lazy eviction — free memory in background thread
lazyfree-lazy-eviction yes
lazyfree-lazy-expire yes
lazyfree-lazy-server-del yes

# Compact encoding thresholds
hash-max-listpack-entries 128       # Hash uses listpack below this field count
hash-max-listpack-value 64          # Hash uses listpack below this value size
list-max-listpack-size -2           # ~8 KB per listpack node
zset-max-listpack-entries 128
zset-max-listpack-value 64
set-max-intset-entries 512
```

Monitor memory usage and eviction rates:

```bash
# Check current memory stats
redis-cli INFO memory | grep -E "used_memory_human|maxmemory_human|mem_fragmentation"

# Watch eviction rate in real-time
redis-cli INFO stats | grep evicted_keys

# Inspect encoding of a specific key
redis-cli OBJECT ENCODING user:42
redis-cli MEMORY USAGE user:42
```

sections.title: Memory Optimization Tips in Java
Key Points
sections.content:
- **`allkeys-lru` for pure caches** — evicts least recently used key regardless of TTL; the right default when all cached data has equal priority and memory is the bottleneck
- **`volatile-lru` for mixed persistent and cache data** — only evicts keys with TTL set; protects persistent data (sessions, locks) from eviction when used on the same Redis instance as cache data
- **`noeviction` for queues and session stores** — rejects writes when memory is full; requires capacity monitoring and alerting; prevents silent data loss at the cost of write failures
- **Hash encoding with ziplist saves memory** — keep Hash fields below 128 and values short to stay in compact ziplist encoding; one Hash key with N fields uses less memory than N separate String keys
- **`MEMORY USAGE key` and `MEMORY DOCTOR`** — diagnose memory consumption per key and get a Redis-generated diagnosis of memory pressure causes; run before scaling up instance size

sections.title: How to explain this in an interview
sections.content:
Memory management is one of the most operationally important aspects of running Redis in production. Redis stores all data in RAM, so running out of memory stops it from accepting new writes — and the eviction policy determines what happens at that point.

**Eviction policies — what to evict when memory is full**
- `allkeys-lru` evicts the least recently used key across all keys — the right default for a cache where all data has equal priority; Redis automatically removes cold data as memory fills
- `volatile-lru` evicts the LRU key only among keys with a TTL set — protects keys without TTL from eviction; useful when the same Redis instance holds both cached data (TTL set) and persistent data (no TTL)
- `noeviction` rejects new writes with an error when memory is full — appropriate for a session store or queue where losing any data would be catastrophic; requires monitoring to prevent hitting the limit
- `allkeys-lfu` evicts the least frequently used key — better than LRU for access patterns where old keys are still popular; Redis 4.0+

**Data structure choices affect memory**
- A Hash with fewer than 128 fields and small values is stored as a compact ziplist in memory — much more memory-efficient than storing each field as a separate String key; `HSET user:123 name Alice email alice@example.com` uses less memory than `SET user:123:name Alice` + `SET user:123:email alice@example.com`
- Lists, Sets, and Sorted Sets also use compact encoding below configured size thresholds; stay below `hash-max-listpack-entries` (128) to keep ziplist encoding

**Key expiry and memory pressure**
- Redis expires keys lazily (checked on access) and actively (periodic scan of a sample of expiring keys) — memory isn't immediately reclaimed when a key's TTL passes; under memory pressure, set aggressive expiry policies
- Use `OBJECT ENCODING key` to check a specific key's encoding; `MEMORY USAGE key` to see how much memory one key consumes; `MEMORY DOCTOR` for a high-level diagnosis of memory issues
